newsitem.title: INDONESIA: FOCUS - Indonesia seen tightening law after Busang.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Indonesia seen tightening law after Busang.

text.p: Indonesia, stung by the Busang gold scandal, is likely to tighten mining regulations and become more wary of small exploration companies in a bid to avoid embarrassment in future, industry officials said on Monday.

"There will be tighter controls...and the government will become very wary of junior mining companies," Graeme Robertson, chairman and chief executive officer of the Swabara Group mining company told Reuters.

Consultant Strathcona Mineral Services Ltd stunned the mining world when it told Canadian exploration company Bre-X Minerals Ltd that geological samples from its Busang discovery had been falsified on a scale "without precedent in the history of mining anywhere in the world".

Strathcona, in a report released in Toronto on Sunday, said it had not found an economic gold deposit in the southeast zone of the Busang property, the area of Borneo claimed by Bre-X to contain about 71 million ounces of gold.
Bre-X has a 45-percent stake in the Busang property, Freeport McMoRan Copper and Gold Inc of the United States has 15 percent and Indonesian interests the rest.

Robertson said as a result of the scandal gold exploration companies, especially those which are publicly-listed, could be required by Indonesia to carry out independent audits on the properties they are exploring.

"The government will no longer rely on information without it being checked independently. At some stage, the government will want an exploration company that reports a certain amount of gold to provide an independent verification of that."
Other industry officials expressed shock at the Strathcona report, adding that the allegation of data falsification was worse than had been been expected from the report.
"I am shocked," M. Simatupang, vice-chairman of the Indonesia Mining Association, told Reuters. "This is the first time I have have heard of such a thing happening," he said.
"It is horrible. How people have been misinformed."
Mines and Energy Minister Ida Bagus Sudjana, answering reporters' questions, said he had not yet seen the report but thought the government would take action if laws had been violated.
Simatupang said the immediate impact of the annoucement would be felt by smaller mining companies who might face difficulty in raising funds for exploration.
"They will find it more difficult to raise money...the junior companies not the big ones," he added.
An Indonesian geologist, who declined to be identified, said he hoped other exploration companies would not be penalised by the government because of the Busang scandal.

He also said the Strathcona report could have implications for 65 contracts issued by the government last Monday to dozens of foreign and local companies to explore the archipelago for minerals -- from gold to copper and nickel.
"Definitely there will be implications," he said, referring to the contracts of work. "It will become very hard for junior mining companies to raise money.
Indonesia had got a "black eye" from the scandal, he said, but the country remained attractive for exploration companies wanting to venture into the mining sector.
"There will be a certain fear when mining companies want to come to Indonesia but the geology is prospective," he said.
